evidenceAudit.scope: Children and adults with acute sore throat in India: separating viral from group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis with the Centor score, deciding who needs antibiotics, and recognising dangerous causes (epiglottitis, deep neck abscess, diphtheria). Built on the ICMR Pharyngitis and Sore Throat workflow (October 2019); maximum doses, penicillin V, benzathine penicillin and penicillin-allergy options from a stewardship algorithm based on AHA 2009 and IDSA 2012.
findings: Causes, bacterial versus viral features, specific syndromes, Centor criteria and actions, red flags, investigations, symptomatic care, amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day for 10 days, macrolide alternatives, airway compromise management and tonsillectomy criteria checked against the ICMR Pharyngitis STW (October 2019).

Maximum doses and alternatives (penicillin V, benzathine penicillin G, cephalexin, clindamycin, azithromycin) and the penicillin-allergy pathway from the Stanford stewardship algorithm (dosing per American Heart Association (AHA) 2009 and Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) 2012).
ICMR and the AHA-based algorithm differ on amoxicillin dosing frequency; shown side by side.
unverifiedSections: Analgesic doses are not given in the Pharyngitis STW; paracetamol and ibuprofen doses are taken from the ICMR Bacterial Skin Infections STW.
Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime and steroid doses for epiglottitis or croup are not given in the STW; follow the airway emergency protocol.
Diphtheria antitoxin and peritonsillar abscess drainage are not covered here; see the diphtheria topic.
The adult doses shown are the algorithm's maximum doses for heavier patients; the ICMR STW gives only the weight-based amoxicillin dose.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Most sore throats are viral and settle within a week. Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (GABHS) is the main bacterial cause; it matters because untreated infection can lead to rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease and glomerulonephritis, which remain important in India (ICMR STW). The Centor score (no cough, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior neck nodes, fever) decides who gets antibiotics. Dangerous causes — epiglottitis, deep neck space abscess, diphtheria and infectious mononucleosis — must not be missed.
keyMechanisms: Viruses or bacteria infect the pharyngeal and tonsillar mucosa, causing inflammation and pain.
GABHS produces exudate, tender nodes and fever without cough.
Cross-reacting antibodies after GABHS can cause rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.
Spread into neck spaces causes abscesses that threaten the airway.

symptoms: Sore throat, painful swallowing, fever (ICMR STW)
Runny nose, red eyes, cough or mouth ulcers suggest a virus (ICMR STW)
Hoarse 'hot potato' voice (abscess) (ICMR STW red flag)
physicalSigns: Tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes (ICMR STW)
Generalised lymph nodes, enlarged liver or spleen (infectious mononucleosis) (ICMR STW)
Grey adherent membrane beyond the tonsils (diphtheria) (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Drooling, high fever, breathing difficulty in a child: epiglottitis (ICMR STW)
Hot potato voice or one-sided tonsil swelling (ICMR STW)
Membrane beyond the tonsils with toxaemia: diphtheria (ICMR STW)
Sore throat with agranulocytosis (for example on antithyroid drugs) (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Smoking and gastro-oesophageal reflux (non-infective sore throat) (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; low or no fever (ICMR STW).
Generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes; rash if given amoxicillin (ICMR STW).
Adherent grey membrane extending beyond tonsils, toxaemia (ICMR STW).
Drooling, stridor or breathing difficulty in children (ICMR STW).
Hot potato voice, one-sided tonsil swelling (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: One point each: no cough; tonsillar exudate; tender anterior cervical lymph nodes; fever.
0–1: no antibiotic. 2–3: antibiotic only if rapid antigen test or throat culture is positive. 4: antibiotic without waiting for tests.
More than 7 episodes in the last year; 5 or more a year for 2 years; or 3 or more a year for 3 years.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Essential test; confirms GABHS for Centor 2–3 (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Look for toxicity, epiglottitis or an oropharyngeal abscess; check hydration (ICMR STW).
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor and feel for neck and generalised nodes (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Symptomatic care
actions: Salt-water gargles, warm drinks, rest (ICMR STW).
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotic decision
actions: Score Centor; treat at 4, test at 2–3, do not treat at 0–1 (ICMR STW).
First choice amoxicillin for 10 days (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Airway compromise
actions: Suspected epiglottitis or croup: parenteral ceftriaxone or cefotaxime and steroids; refer (ICMR STW).
Manage deep neck space infection, diphtheria, epiglottitis and croup at district hospital (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Recurrent tonsillitis
actions: Refer for tonsillectomy if episode criteria are met (ICMR STW).

medicationPlan.note: ICMR STW: amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day for 10 days, erythromycin or azithromycin if penicillin-allergic. Maximum doses and other alternatives are from the Stanford algorithm (AHA 2009 dosing), which strongly discourages non-penicillin alternatives unless needed. Analgesic doses from the ICMR Bacterial Skin Infections STW. Not clinically reviewed.

learningObjectives: Use the Centor score to decide on antibiotics.
Choose and dose the right antibiotic.
Recognise airway and diphtheria red flags.
keyPoints: Drooling or breathing difficulty in a child: airway emergency.
Membrane beyond the tonsils: think diphtheria.
pitfalls: Short courses of penicillin for GABHS (10 days needed).
Examining the throat of a child with suspected epiglottitis outside a safe setting.
